title: Miranda v. Arizona
text:
SYLLABUS

The prosecution may not use statements stemming from custodial interrogation of a defendant unless it demonstrates the use of procedural safeguards effective to secure the privilege against self-incrimination.

I. Background

Ernesto Miranda was arrested and questioned by police officers for two hours without being advised of his right to counsel or his right to remain silent. He signed a written confession that was admitted at trial over objection, and he was convicted of kidnapping and rape.

II. Holding

We hold that when an individual is taken into custody and subjected to questioning, the privilege against self-incrimination is jeopardized. Prior to any questioning, the person must be warned that he has a right to remain silent, that any statement he does make may be used as evidence against him, and that he has a right to the presence of an attorney, either retained or appointed. The defendant may waive these rights, provided the waiver is made voluntarily, knowingly and intelligently. Unless and until such warnings and waiver are demonstrated by the prosecution at trial, no evidence obtained as a result of interrogation can be used against him.

III. Disposition

The judgment of the Supreme Court of Arizona is reversed.

title: Carpenter v. United States
text:
SYLLABUS

The Government's acquisition of historical cell-site location records is a Fourth Amendment search, and accessing seven days or more of such records requires a warrant supported by probable cause.

I. Background

Prosecutors obtained months of cell-site location information from Timothy Carpenter's wireless carriers under the Stored Communications Act, which requires only reasonable grounds to believe the records are relevant to an investigation. The records placed his phone near four robberies.

II. Analysis

A person does not surrender all Fourth Amendment protection by venturing into the public sphere. Historical cell-site records present even greater privacy concerns than GPS monitoring of a vehicle: they give the Government near perfect surveillance and allow it to travel back in time to retrace a person's whereabouts. The third-party doctrine of Smith and Miller does not extend to the qualitatively different category of cell-site records, which are not truly shared in any voluntary sense.

III. Holding

Before compelling a wireless carrier to turn over a subscriber's historical cell-site location information, the Government's obligation is a familiar one: get a warrant. The judgment of the Court of Appeals is reversed.

title: Terry v. Ohio
text:
SYLLABUS

A police officer may stop and frisk a person for weapons where the officer has reasonable suspicion, based on specific and articulable facts, that criminal activity may be afoot and that the person may be armed and dangerous.

I. Background

A veteran detective observed two men repeatedly walking past and peering into a store window, conferring after each pass. Suspecting they were casing the store for a robbery, he approached, identified himself, and patted down their outer clothing, discovering revolvers.

II. Analysis

The Fourth Amendment governs seizures of the person short of a technical arrest. Whenever a police officer accosts an individual and restrains his freedom to walk away, he has seized that person, and a careful exploration of the outer surfaces of clothing is a search. But the reasonableness of a protective frisk is judged by balancing the need to search against the invasion the search entails. An officer need not be certain the individual is armed; the issue is whether a reasonably prudent man in the circumstances would be warranted in the belief that his safety or that of others was in danger.

III. Disposition

The revolver seized from Terry was properly admitted in evidence. Affirmed.

title: Brady v. Maryland
text:
SYLLABUS

Suppression by the prosecution of evidence favorable to an accused who has requested it violates due process where the evidence is material either to guilt or to punishment, irrespective of the good faith or bad faith of the prosecution.

I. Background

Brady and a companion were separately tried for murder. Brady admitted participating in the crime but claimed his companion did the actual killing. The prosecution withheld the companion's extrajudicial statement in which he admitted the homicide, and Brady learned of it only after his conviction was affirmed.

II. Holding

Society wins not only when the guilty are convicted but when criminal trials are fair; our system of the administration of justice suffers when any accused is treated unfairly. A prosecution that withholds evidence on demand of an accused which, if made available, would tend to exculpate him or reduce the penalty helps shape a trial that bears heavily on the defendant. That casts the prosecutor in the role of an architect of a proceeding that does not comport with standards of justice.

III. Disposition

The judgment is affirmed as to the remand on the question of punishment.

title: Harlow v. Fitzgerald
text:
SYLLABUS

Government officials performing discretionary functions are shielded from liability for civil damages insofar as their conduct does not violate clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known.

I. Background

A discharged Air Force analyst sued senior White House aides for civil damages, alleging retaliatory dismissal for congressional testimony. The aides claimed absolute immunity, and in the alternative qualified immunity, from suit.

II. Analysis

The resolution of immunity questions inherently requires a balance between the evils inevitable in any available alternative. Insubstantial suits against government officials exact heavy social costs: the expenses of litigation, the diversion of official energy from pressing public issues, and the deterrence of able citizens from acceptance of public office. Reliance on the objective reasonableness of an official's conduct, as measured by reference to clearly established law, should avoid excessive disruption of government and permit the resolution of many insubstantial claims on summary judgment.

III. Holding

Bare allegations of malice should not suffice to subject government officials either to the costs of trial or to the burdens of broad-reaching discovery. If the law at the time was not clearly established, an official could not reasonably be expected to anticipate subsequent legal developments, nor could he fairly be said to know that the law forbade conduct not previously identified as unlawful.

title: Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council
text:
SYLLABUS

When a court reviews an agency's construction of the statute which it administers, it must first ask whether Congress has directly spoken to the precise question at issue; if the statute is silent or ambiguous, the question is whether the agency's answer is based on a permissible construction of the statute.

I. Background

The Clean Air Act Amendments require permits for new or modified major stationary sources of air pollution. The EPA adopted a regulation allowing a State to treat all pollution-emitting devices within an industrial grouping as though they were encased within a single bubble, so that a plant may install or modify one piece of equipment without a permit if the alteration does not increase total plantwide emissions.

II. Analysis

If Congress has explicitly left a gap for the agency to fill, there is an express delegation of authority to the agency to elucidate a specific provision of the statute by regulation, and such legislative regulations are given controlling weight unless they are arbitrary, capricious, or manifestly contrary to the statute. Federal judges, who have no constituency, have a duty to respect legitimate policy choices made by those who do.

III. Holding

The EPA's definition of the term source is a permissible construction of the statute that seeks to accommodate progress in reducing air pollution with economic growth. Reversed.

title: Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District
text:
SYLLABUS

Students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate; school officials may not prohibit expression without evidence that it would materially and substantially disrupt the work and discipline of the school.

I. Background

A group of students planned to wear black armbands to school to publicize their objections to the hostilities in Vietnam. The school districts adopted a policy that any student wearing an armband would be asked to remove it and suspended if he refused. The petitioners wore armbands, were sent home, and sued.

II. Analysis

The wearing of an armband for the purpose of expressing certain views is the type of symbolic act that is within the Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment. Undifferentiated fear or apprehension of disturbance is not enough to overcome the right to freedom of expression. In our system, state-operated schools may not be enclaves of totalitarianism; students may not be regarded as closed-circuit recipients of only that which the State chooses to communicate.

III. Disposition

The record does not demonstrate any facts which might reasonably have led school authorities to forecast substantial disruption. Reversed and remanded.

title: Kelo v. City of New London
text:
SYLLABUS

A city's exercise of eminent domain in furtherance of an economic development plan satisfies the public use requirement of the Fifth Amendment.

I. Background

The city of New London approved an integrated development plan designed to revitalize its ailing economy, and its development agent purchased property and sought to acquire the remaining parcels from unwilling owners by eminent domain. The owners' properties were not blighted; they were condemned only because they happened to be located in the development area.

II. Analysis

The Court long ago rejected any literal requirement that condemned property be put into use for the general public. When this Court began applying the Fifth Amendment to the States, it embraced the broader and more natural interpretation of public use as public purpose. Promoting economic development is a traditional and long accepted function of government, and there is no principled way of distinguishing economic development from the other public purposes that the Court has recognized.

III. Holding

The city's proposed disposition of the petitioners' property qualifies as a public use within the meaning of the Takings Clause. The judgment of the Supreme Court of Connecticut is affirmed.

title: Gideon v. Wainwright
text:
SYLLABUS

The Sixth Amendment right to the assistance of counsel is a fundamental right essential to a fair trial and is made obligatory upon the States by the Fourteenth Amendment; an indigent defendant in a criminal prosecution has the right to appointed counsel.

I. Background

Gideon was charged in a Florida state court with breaking and entering a poolroom with intent to commit a misdemeanor, a felony under Florida law. Appearing without funds and without a lawyer, he asked the court to appoint counsel; the request was denied on the ground that state law permitted appointment only in capital cases. He conducted his own defense and was convicted.

II. Analysis

Governments, both state and federal, quite properly spend vast sums of money to establish machinery to try defendants accused of crime. Lawyers to prosecute are everywhere deemed essential to protect the public's interest in an orderly society. That government hires lawyers to prosecute and defendants who have the money hire lawyers to defend are the strongest indications of the widespread belief that lawyers in criminal courts are necessities, not luxuries.

III. Disposition

Betts v. Brady is overruled. The judgment is reversed and the cause remanded.

title: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan
text:
SYLLABUS

A public official may not recover damages for a defamatory falsehood relating to his official conduct unless he proves that the statement was made with actual malice, that is, with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.

I. Background

An elected commissioner of Montgomery, Alabama brought a civil libel action against four clergymen and the New York Times over a full-page advertisement describing a wave of terror against civil rights demonstrators. Some statements in the advertisement were inaccurate, and a jury awarded five hundred thousand dollars in damages.

II. Analysis

We consider this case against the background of a profound national commitment to the principle that debate on public issues should be uninhibited, robust, and wide-open, and that it may well include vehement, caustic, and sometimes unpleasantly sharp attacks on government and public officials. Erroneous statement is inevitable in free debate, and it must be protected if the freedoms of expression are to have the breathing space that they need to survive.

III. Holding

The rule of law applied by the Alabama courts is constitutionally deficient for failure to provide the safeguards for freedom of speech and of the press that are required by the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Reversed and remanded.

title: Katz v. United States
text:
SYLLABUS

The Fourth Amendment protects people, not places; the Government's electronic interception of a conversation made from a public telephone booth is a search and seizure requiring a warrant.

I. Background

Katz was convicted of transmitting wagering information by telephone across state lines. FBI agents had attached an electronic listening and recording device to the outside of the public telephone booth from which he placed his calls, and his end of the conversations was introduced at trial.

II. Analysis

What a person knowingly exposes to the public, even in his own home or office, is not a subject of Fourth Amendment protection. But what he seeks to preserve as private, even in an area accessible to the public, may be constitutionally protected. One who occupies a telephone booth, shuts the door behind him, and pays the toll that permits him to place a call is surely entitled to assume that the words he utters into the mouthpiece will not be broadcast to the world.

III. Holding

The Government's activities in electronically listening to and recording the petitioner's words violated the privacy upon which he justifiably relied while using the telephone booth. Searches conducted without prior judicial approval are per se unreasonable, subject only to a few specifically established exceptions. Reversed.

title: Batson v. Kentucky
text:
SYLLABUS

The Equal Protection Clause forbids a prosecutor from challenging potential jurors solely on account of their race; a defendant may establish a prima facie case of purposeful discrimination in the selection of the petit jury solely on evidence concerning the prosecutor's exercise of peremptory challenges at the defendant's trial.

I. Background

During the criminal trial of a Black defendant, the prosecutor used peremptory challenges to strike all four Black persons on the venire, and a jury composed only of white persons was selected. Defense counsel moved to discharge the jury; the trial judge denied the motion.

II. Analysis

Purposeful racial discrimination in selection of the venire violates a defendant's right to equal protection because it denies him the protection that a trial by jury is intended to secure. Once the defendant makes a prima facie showing, the burden shifts to the State to come forward with a neutral explanation for challenging the jurors; the prosecutor may not rebut the defendant's case merely by denying a discriminatory motive.

III. Disposition

The judgment is reversed and the case remanded for further proceedings.
